name: Intercommunalism
summary: Intercommunalism is Huey P. Newton's 1970 theory, adopted by the Black Panther Party, that US-led imperialism has turned the world's nations into dependent communities, so nationalism and internationalism are both obsolete. It calls on the world's communities to seize the means of production and share the world's wealth and technology, passing through revolutionary intercommunalism before a stateless communism. In the interim it urges free community survival programs, built on the Marxist dialectical method.
scope: Newton's theory as set out from the September 1970 Revolutionary People's Constitutional Convention to his 1971-72 writings and his unpublished 1974 text, as the scholars Narayan and Vasquez present it (s3, s4, s5): reactionary intercommunalism as the imperial stage, revolutionary intercommunalism as the people's stage, and survival pending revolution. It excludes the Black Panther Party's earlier black nationalist and revolutionary nationalist phases, and does not stand for the Party's other positions that Newton did not tie to the theory.

notes: The record is one thinker's work, so the set of answers is thin; unanswered statements are ones Newton's intercommunalist texts (1970-72) and the three scholarly accounts never address. Themes searched in To Die for the People and the Boston speech: economy, government and elections, courts and law, police and prisons, religion, race, women and sexuality (the August 1970 essay predates the theory and was left out), war and alliances, the UN, immigration and borders, technology, ecology and culture. Newton's position on Black capitalism changed in 1971 (blanket condemnation, then conditional support for community-minded Black businesses), so statements on it are left null. A 1974 Newton text and his Yale talks were not available in full.
